name: Confederate States of America
info: The unrecognised republic of eleven seceded Southern states, formed in 1861 to safeguard slavery, which fought the United States for four years until Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865.

facts.capital: Montgomery, Alabama (4 February – 29 May 1861); Richmond, Virginia (from 30 May 1861); Danville for eight days in April 1865
facts.founder: The Montgomery Convention of the seceded Deep South states, 4–8 February 1861; Jefferson Davis, provisional and then permanent president
facts.predecessor: Seven slave states of the United States that passed secession ordinances between 20 December 1860 and 1 February 1861, joined by four more after Fort Sumter
facts.successor: The United States, which readmitted the states to Congress during Reconstruction after each ratified the Thirteenth Amendment

t: Historians widely agree that preserving slavery was the principal aim of secession, as the states' own secession documents show; in 1860 enslaved people were 39 per cent of the eleven states' population and 31 per cent of free households owned slaves.

Its permanent constitution copied much of the United States Constitution verbatim but added explicit protections for slavery in every territory, forbade any state to bar slaveholders from bringing their slaves in, and kept the ban on the African slave trade.

Outnumbered about four to one in military manpower and far more in industry and railroads, the Confederacy passed the first national conscription in North America on 16 April 1862, financed itself by printing money until flour cost $100 a barrel in Richmond, and won recognition from no foreign government.
dyk: No foreign government ever recognised the Confederacy: when Ambrose Dudley Mann reported a letter from Pope Pius IX addressed to "the Illustrious and Honorable Jefferson Davis, President of the Confederate States of America", Secretary of State Judah P. Benjamin replied that Mann had mistranslated it and that it was "a mere inferential recognition".
ev: On 20 December South Carolina votes unanimously for secession after Abraham Lincoln's election; Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas follow by 1 February 1861.
On 8 February delegates at the Montgomery Convention form the Confederate States of America; Jefferson Davis is elected provisional president the next day.
On 12 April Confederate forces under Beauregard bombard and take Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor; Lincoln calls up 75,000 militia and Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina secede.
Davis is inaugurated under the permanent constitution for a six-year term; the Permanent Congress has opened in Richmond on 18 February.
On 16 April the Confederate Congress imposes the first mass conscription on North American territory, making white men from 18 to 35 soldiers for three years.
Lee's invasion of Maryland is turned back at Antietam and Bragg's of Kentucky fails; Lincoln's preliminary Emancipation Proclamation ends British and French thoughts of recognition.
Vicksburg and Port Hudson fall, closing the Mississippi, and Lee's strike into Pennsylvania is repulsed at Gettysburg; the Confederacy withdraws into an interior defence.
On 9 April Richmond having fallen when Lee's lines broke at Petersburg, Lee surrenders at Appomattox Court House; Davis is captured on 10 May and the last land forces surrender by June.

sections.foundation:
The Confederacy was made by secession. Whether slavery might spread into the Western territories had become the defining political issue of the mid nineteenth century. Abraham Lincoln's election in November 1860 brought declarations of secession from seven slave states of the Deep South whose cotton economies depended on enslaved labour: South Carolina on 20 December 1860, unanimously, then Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana and Texas by 1 February 1861, none of them unanimous. Historians widely agree that preserving slavery was their principal aim, and the Lost Cause claim that slavery was not the cause is contradicted by the secession documents themselves.

Their conventions sent delegates to Montgomery, Alabama, on 4 February 1861. A provisional government was formed on 8 February, Jefferson Davis and Alexander H. Stephens were elected provisional president and vice-president unanimously, and the Permanent Constitution was adopted on 12 March. Lincoln took office on 4 March; the Buchanan and Lincoln administrations kept the federal forts, and on 12 April 1861 Beauregard's guns forced the surrender of Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor. Lincoln's call for 75,000 militia followed on 15 April, and Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina seceded between April and May. The capital moved to Richmond on 30 May 1861, a show of defiance in the state that had the largest military-aged white population and the most resources.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Confederacy was a plantation economy with white ownership and an enslaved labour force. Its plantations supplied two-thirds of the world's cotton; planters put their profits into more slaves and fresh land as cotton exhausted the soil. By the 1860 census the eleven states held about three million enslaved people, 39 per cent of their population, and 31 per cent of free households owned slaves; free Black people were 2 per cent. There was little manufacturing or mining, $155 million of goods in 1860, and the industrial border cities of Baltimore, Wheeling, Louisville and St. Louis never came under Confederate control.

War wrecked the economy. Southerners stopped cotton exports in early 1861 to force European support, the King Cotton strategy, and failed: Britain had stocks for a year and other sources. The Union blockade then ended commercial shipping, and the government, afraid of hard taxes and collecting only $3.5 million in tariffs in its whole life, financed the war by printing $1.5 billion in notes, which became worthless. By April 1863 flour cost $100 a barrel in Richmond and poor women rioted for food there, in Atlanta and in other cities. Historians agree there were no slave insurrections, but enslaved people grew more independent, spied for the North and ran in large numbers to federal lines, and after the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 over 200,000 freed people worked for the federal army, eventually as soldiers.
sections.military:
The Confederate States Army, Navy and Marine Corps were created by the Provisional Congress from 28 February 1861 and numbered perhaps 750,000 to 1,000,000 men over the war; some 94,000 were killed or mortally wounded, 164,000 died of disease and 26,000 to 31,000 in Union prison camps. The North outnumbered it about four to one in manpower and far more in equipment, industry and railroads. The victories of 1861 could not be followed up for want of supply and fresh troops. When one-year enlistments expired the army was allowed to disband for two months in early 1862, and on 16 April 1862 Congress passed the first American law of national conscription, extended in September to men of 45 and in February 1864 to all from 17 to 50.

Strategy was defensive: dispersal to satisfy the governors with a concentration around Richmond. In 1862 New Orleans fell on 29 April, and the two invasions of Kentucky and Maryland ended at Antietam, which Allan Nevins calls the strategic high-water mark. Chancellorsville in April 1863 was followed by the loss of Vicksburg and Port Hudson and the repulse at Gettysburg in July, then Chattanooga; by early 1864 the government controlled 53 per cent of its population, and Sherman's march to Savannah and Grant's siege of Petersburg followed. Lee, as he wrote, lacked reserves to turn victories into the destruction of an army. In 1865 he surrendered at Appomattox on 9 April.
sections.governance:
The Montgomery Convention adopted a first constitution of a confederation of "sovereign and independent states", then in March 1861 a permanent one establishing a federal government, which took effect on 22 February 1862. Much of it copied the United States Constitution verbatim, but it explicitly protected slavery in any territory, forbade states to bar slaveholders from other states from bringing in their slaves, kept the ban on importing "Negroes of the African race", and gave the president a six-year term without re-election and a line-item veto. Jefferson Davis, the only president, and Alexander H. Stephens were elected unopposed on 6 November 1861.

The Provisional Congress sat as a unicameral body with one vote per state; the Permanent Congress, elected for 18 February 1862, had a Senate of 26 and a House of 106 apportioned by free and slave populations, and sat in six sessions until 18 March 1865. There were no political parties, which David M. Potter judged did real and direct damage, since no alternative to Davis's conduct of the war could form. The Supreme Court provided for in the constitution was never seated, states-rights advocates resisting its appellate power over state courts; district courts under judges appointed by Davis heard prize and sequestration cases. The army arrested at least 4,108 men suspected of Union loyalty, and East Tennessee's attempt to secede from the Confederacy was checked by martial law.
sections.impact:
The Confederacy's reach abroad was slight. It sent James M. Mason to London and John Slidell to Paris, but neither won recognition or military aid. Lord John Russell, Napoleon III and Gladstone toyed with recognition or mediation until Antietam and the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation of September 1862 ended it; British opinion, proud of ending the slave trade and taught by Frederick Douglass and other Black abolitionists, was against the Confederacy except in Liverpool. In December 1864 Davis secretly sent Duncan F. Kenner to offer to sacrifice slavery for recognition, but Europe saw the Confederacy near defeat.

At home its legacy was long. Reconstruction readmitted the states after they ratified the Thirteenth Amendment, which outlawed slavery "except as a punishment for crime"; in Texas v. White (1869) the Supreme Court ruled that no state could unilaterally secede, and in Sprott v. United States (1874) that the Confederacy's foundation was treason. After 1877 Democratic legislatures excluded most Black people and many poor whites from the vote until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The Lost Cause, cultivated by former generals, the United Daughters of the Confederacy and the Sons of Confederate Veterans in the decades after the war and again during the civil rights movement, built monuments and shaped textbooks to sustain white supremacist policies such as the Jim Crow laws; the battle flag's modern display began with the segregationist Dixiecrats in 1948.
sections.decline:
The Confederacy lost ground in every campaign after 1862. In early 1864 it still held 53 per cent of its population, but Sherman's March to the Sea took Savannah, Grant besieged Lee at Petersburg. Civilians who had been enthusiastic in 1861–62 had by 1864 lost faith and looked to protect their homes. Desertion grew, conscription produced as many evasions as soldiers, and the railroads, never planned for or protected, stood on the verge of collapse. In the first months of 1865 the Carolinas campaign devastated the heartland, Sheridan held the Shenandoah breadbasket, and Wilmington, the last blockade-running port, fell.

By then the Confederacy controlled no ports or navigable rivers, its administration survived in three pockets holding a third of its people, and its armies were defeated or disbanding. At the Hampton Roads Conference in February 1865 its officials refused Lincoln's offer of reunion with compensation for emancipated slaves; Davis's policy was independence or nothing. When the Union broke Lee's lines at Petersburg Richmond fell at once, the government fled to Danville for eight days, and Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865. Davis was captured on 10 May and all remaining land forces had surrendered by June. The South had used up about half its capital stock, more than 250,000 of its soldiers were dead, and the billions invested in human property had vanished with slavery itself.

summary: The Confederate States of America, formed in February 1861 by slave states that seceded after Lincoln's election to safeguard slavery, wrote its protection into a constitution otherwise copied from the Union's, fought a four-year war against a foe four times its size, won no foreign recognition, and collapsed with Lee's surrender at Appomattox on 9 April 1865.
references: Emory M. Thomas, The Confederate Nation, 1861–1865 (Harper & Row, 1979)
William C. Davis, Look Away! A History of the Confederate States of America (Free Press, 2002)
Eric J. Wittenberg, Edmund A. Sargus Jr. and Penny L. Barrick, Seceding from Secession: The Civil War, Politics, and the Creation of West Virginia (Savas Beatie, 2020)

pointDescs.1861: Seven, then eleven states secede; the Confederacy is formed at Montgomery on 8 February, takes Fort Sumter on 12 April, moves its capital to Richmond and wins at First Bull Run and Wilson's Creek, though it cannot follow up.
pointDescs.1862: The strategic high-water mark by Allan Nevins's reckoning: Lee drives McClellan from Richmond and wins Second Bull Run and Fredericksburg, but New Orleans falls, conscription begins, and the invasions of Kentucky and Maryland fail at Antietam, after which Britain and France drop recognition.
pointDescs.1863: Chancellorsville is followed by the loss of Vicksburg, Port Hudson and the Mississippi and the repulse at Gettysburg in July; Chattanooga is yielded and the war is henceforth fought inside the South.
pointDescs.1864: Holding 53 per cent of its population at the year's start, the Confederacy loses Atlanta and Savannah to Sherman, Mobile Bay and Nashville, while Lee is besieged at Petersburg and civilians lose faith.
pointDescs.1865: Wilmington, Charleston and Richmond fall; Lee surrenders at Appomattox on 9 April, Congress has adjourned on 18 March and Davis is captured on 10 May.

notes: The curve has five points, not the guide's eight: the state lasted from 1861 to 1865 and the points are integer years, so one per year is the most the format allows. Each description gathers that year's dated events from the article.

The article's only listed work is the Further reading entry (Wittenberg, Sargus and Barrick 2020); its References and Sources sections are empty in the saved text, so there is one reference rather than three.
The article dates Antietam both to 'October 1862' (Military strategy) and to 'September 1862' (Diplomacy and Incursions); September is used.
Strength is the Confederacy's own, scaled to its 1862 peak; 1861 is set at 7 because the state was still forming and the four Upper South states joined only in April–May.
The article gives the Union's name for First Bull Run and the Confederate 'First Manassas'; the profile uses First Bull Run, the name used first in the article.

The Confederacy's founding purpose is stated as the article and the secession documents state it: the preservation of slavery. Lost Cause claims are reported only as what mainstream historians reject.

Left out for space: Kentucky's and Missouri's rival governments, the Arizona Territory campaign of 1862 and the Indian Territory treaties of 12 July 1861 (mentioned only as congressional seats), the Confederate Post Office, the flags, the churches' schisms, Henry Wirz's execution.
